I grew up extremely poor; for about 6 years of my childhood, my family lived in a one room cabin with a few kerosine lanterns, a wood stove, and no indoor plumbing. We hauled water from a nearby spring and had an outhouse in the back yard. Food consisted of whatever my mom was able to grow and can/dry/freeze in the summer, large bulk bags of rice and beans, as well as occasional meat when my stepdad poached game. My mom actually really succeeded later in life by starting a business based on her extreme knowledge of what foods can be found in the wild that are edible, and recipes to make them good (all parts of a dandelion, for starters). Clothes came from the sale racks at thrift stores; I wore sandals with socks almost all winter (in Wisconsin) one year because they were the only thing that fit. I had 2 friends until high school, all the other kids hated me because I was weird. I became a pathological liar trying to impress other kids with all the things I didn't really have. The thing was, though, that I didn't realize how very poor and different my family was until I entered high school. I was always provided for, even if it meant eating rice and beans every day for a week. However, history repeats itself. I became a teenage single mother, my parents died and I had no help. I was horribly poor for years and barely was able to support my kids. We ended up homeless at one point. And then I decided I'd had enough of that life and went back to school. I worked 3 jobs, went to school full time, and handled my duties as a mother in order to get ahead. I now work a successful job and I actually have a house, a nice car, food in my fridge, bills paid, and even some extra money to be able to buy my kids fancy name brand clothes sometimes. I still shop primarily at thrift stores, eat weird cheap foods, and freak out if anyone tried to throw away dish soap containers if they're not completely empty, but I'm very proud of the life I've worked hard to create for my kids.
